summary: This work presents a year-long longitudinal characterization of 27 frequency-tunable transmon qubits across four thermal cycles, revealing a clear stability hierarchy: intrinsic device parameters (qubit frequency and baseline $T_1$) remain robust with $|\Delta f_{01}^{\mathrm{max}}| < 0.5\%$, while environmental variables (flux offsets and two-level system defect distributions) undergo stochastic reconfiguration. Through frequency-dependent relaxation spectroscopy and a novel $T_1$ Spectral Topography Fidelity metric, the authors demonstrate that each thermal cycle acts as a 'hard reset' of the defect landscape, inducing spectral randomization equivalent to $>1000$ hours of continuous low-temperature evolution.
motivation: Superconducting quantum processors require repeated thermal cycling for maintenance and upgrades, yet systematic studies quantifying the impact on device stability and qubit parameters have been absent. Understanding how thermal cycles affect both intrinsic hardware quality and the microscopic TLS environment is essential for developing maintenance strategies for scalable systems.
method: The authors tracked 27 qubits over nine months across four thermal cycles using flux-dependent spectroscopy, $T_1$ measurements, and frequency-dependent relaxation spectroscopy. They introduced a Z-score normalized metric ($\rho = \alpha/\delta$) to quantify reproducibility of the qubit's time-frequency decay landscape, comparing intra-cycle and inter-cycle spectral fingerprints.
result: Qubit frequencies deviate by $\pm 20$ MHz ($0.5\%$ relative) and $T_1$ baselines show no degradation across cycles, confirming fabrication robustness. Conversely, flux biases and TLS distributions randomize after each cycle with $\rho \sim 0.3$ (inter-cycle) versus $\rho \sim 0.8$ (initial intra-cycle), matching fidelity levels observed after $>1000$ hours of continuous diffusion at 20 mK.
